newsitem.title: UK: Chase looks to Yankees as T-note yields wallow.
newsitem.headline: Chase looks to Yankees as T-note yields wallow.

text.p: Chase Asset Management is broadening its scope in the U.S. fixed income market as it becomes harder to squeeze value from range-bound Treasuries, a Chase investment executive said on Friday.

Susan Huang, head of U.S. fixed income for Chase Asset Management, said Chase had raised its weighting in Yankee and global bonds and the asset-backed sector. Yankee bonds are U.S. dollar-bonds issued in the U.S. by a foreign borrower.
"We're taking advantage of other sectors in the market that offer better value," Huang said in an interview with Reuters in London.
"We really like Yankees and globals. We are also very, very bullish on the asset-backed markets."

Despite concerns about robust growth and inflation in the U.S., government bonds have largely been trading in a range since March last year. The yield on the benchmark long bond has vascillated between just under 6.5 percent and 7.3 percent.
A typical Chase U.S. bond portfolio contains around 30-35 percent Treasuries, 20-25 percent corporate and Yankee bonds and the remaining in mortgage and asset-backed bonds, Huang said.
She said Chase's exposure to Yankees has increased to around five percent from two percent in the fourth quarter of 1996.
Supply and liquidity of Yankees were expected to continue to pick up, with issues expected from southeast Asia and Malaysia in particular, Huang said.
She said mortgage-backed securities were also attractive.

"We see that as an area where there is increasing demand from overseas institutional investors because it has no credit risk," she said. Mortgage-backed securities such as those issued by agencies like Fannie Mae are guaranteed by the U.S. government.
Huang said domestic investors were turning to these areaa for yield, but foreign investors still preferred government bonds. Central banks were still among the biggest buyers of U.S. Treasuries.

Huang expected Treasuries to have trouble in the next few weeks ahead of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony and the Federal Open Market Committee meeting on March 25.

But thereafter, the tone would improve and Chase would begin to put on curve-flattening trades. She saw U.S. growth slowing to around 2.0 percent in the first quarter from 4.7 percent in the fourth quarter and the Fed holding interest rates steady through the year.

In such an environment, the yield on the long bond might be able to squeak below its long-held range to around 6.5 percent, but investors were better advised looking to more interesting areas of the U.S. fixed-income sector, said Huang.
